title: Ask HN: What are the most useful, concrete AI skills to independently learn?
content:
Comments
Specifically, what are the most useful, concrete skills to learn as an individual to take economic advantage of the advances in LLMs, agents and associated new technological capabilities?

What is accessible to learn just from the internet and experimentation, without a degree program, assuming a preexisting moderately technical background? The clearer and more specific (eg. “Learn how-to x with y”) the better.

Thank you!

indiehackers1 · Nov 14, 2026

Get a 7B model running locally before you touch any API.

A quantized 7B is around 4.7GB and runs on a 16GB laptop with no GPU, via llama.cpp. The cost saving is not the point. The point is that you can run the same input seven times in an hour and watch what actually changes. Once you have seen your own quantization and sampling settings move the output, API models stop being magic and become a config you can reason about.

Second skill nobody lists: writing loops that fail loudly. Long generations die silently - the stream just stops and your code sits there waiting. I spent days convinced my model was bad before I added a watchdog and per-run logs. The model was fine. My plumbing was not.

Both are weekend-sized, no degree needed. And the people making money off this right now are not the ones with the cleverest prompts, they are the ones who can tell a model failure from a pipeline failure.

suprjami · Nov 14, 2026

Watch the 3Blue1Brown YouTube series on machine learning. Understand how these things work and that they are not magical all-knowing answer machines or even anything intelligent - they are next-most-likely-word predictors. That's all. Demistify and keep that in mind with everything you do afterwards.

I presume you don't want to drop thousands of dollars on video cards so pay Sam/Dario your 20 bucks a month.

Ask the LLM to build things you have already done before. You need to know the correct answer so you can evaluate the solution the LLM provides you.

Start with single-file scripts you have written, you can do this in just the ChatGPT or Claude web interface. Start with a vague prompt which doesn't specify many constraints or details. See what they get right and wrong. Try being much more specific and detailed. Make it ask you questions about what you want before it starts work.

Try the small/old/dumb model with no thinking and try the big/new/smart model with full thinking and notice the difference in capability.

Learn to setup an agent software in a sandbox of some kind. I prefer Pi in a Podman container, with only access to the project directory, but there are a million options out there these days.

From this agent software, ask for explanations on a codebase you already know. Again the purpose is to know the answer in advance so you can evaluate the response provided. Ask it to just tell you some answers. Ask it to give you a code flow and reference to read more yourself.

Build something larger, like a program across multiple files. Again try being vague and being specific, see the difference in what it spits out.

Use it to troubleshoot a problem you have solved, like your favourite bug, and also just a boring regular bug. Try different types of issue.

Learn to create an AGENTS.md for a project or SKILL.md for reusable instructions anywhere, but don't stuff it full of useless nonsense you think the model needs. Build it from experience of only what the thing gets wrong.

Some people say you can ask LLMs to write their own md files, but imo these things generate way too much text. You could ask it to do that as a starting point then trim it down to remove all the extra unnecessary verbose crap.

Through all this, try asking it the same thing multiple times in different new sessions. Notice the answers vary. Sometimes it gets it wrong and sometimes right. Same question, same model, same everything, different answer.

Notice you need to know the right answer to evaluate the response. In situations where you don't know the answer yourself, hopefully you've seen enough wrong answers now to not trust it. Use these things to guide your own investigation, like the exercise above where you asked for code flow and references to read yourself. I think of this as "LLM as search engine, not answer engine".

That seems to be 95% of what people use these things for. This set of skills would have been useful for the last 18 months and seems to be the way the industry momentum is moving at the moment.

lmf4lol · Nov 14, 2026

I personally would say: Learn how to think like an engineer. As in:

- Be able to analyze a situation into processes and discrete steps

- Be able to describe the actual (!) problem you want to be solved

- Be able to describe how to verify that the problem is actually solved

- Be able to ask the right questions regarding HOW the problem has been solved in order to gain understanding and to identify the next steps and improvements

- Be able to identify when the AI gets stuck or down a rabbit hole and to guide it out of there.

- Understand what LLMs are good at and what they are not good at. And there are tons of things they are not good at.

Disclaimer: This is absoluty not based on any scientific study or so :-) Just my personal experience! Feel free to disagree.

But my experience comes directly from my work: I have a lot of customers on my platform that are not engineers, but make use of AI to solve business problems through automations. Nearly everytime when they are stuck (or burning through a sh*tload of tokens in no time), it is because one of those skills aren't present. So I try to teach them more and more how to "think like an engineer". And often when it lands, they become much better at using AI in a very short time. The best learners are often those that already had some kind of engineering background.

Now granted, the frontier models can help themselves pretty well and often can produce amazing results with very bad input. But they are also expensive. If you work with less-than-frontier, those skill requirements become very salient again. And thats what we do. We mostly work with models like Deepseek flash or GLM Flash or even local ones like Qwen3.7 .

Learn communication styles. You could use this model: https://www.leaderfactor.com/learn/four-leadership-styles/

Sometimes you'll be coaching, others delegating, and on the agent's worst days you'll be directing.

You can flex between them: for example start in a high trust mode, using an open ended communication style with the agent - thenif the work sucks shift to a more direct / blunt style. Try to avoid asking for exactly what you want, though. Working through curiosity and guiding questions gives the agent its best chance to surprise you - and an open ended conversation could uncover solutions you hadn't thought of.

The most modern efficient slopftware factories are bottlenecked trying to get things out the door.

That's a huge opportunity for you.

Learn the many techniques the industry has developed for scaling verification.

I don't mean infra; CI is solved. I mean Red-green & test-driven development, the testing pyramid (most unit tests/fewer functional/integration tests/happy-path e2e tests), learn how to get the most out of tools like Playwright and test frameworks like pytest and vitest and go and rust's testing tooling. Learn to scale verification, and you'll solve your team's biggest bottleneck.

hypendev · Nov 14, 2026

I'd rank them like this - this comes from applying LLM's since GPT-3 autocomplete API, teaching people how to use them, giving talks to developers, answering their questions, training my own models and seeing how people interact with them:

1. Building your own model - this will cost you a bit, but is without a doubt the best way to earn concrete AI skills. From picking the data to training, seeing how it evolves, improves and scales. You will understand the "hyperplanes" of a model's inner world better than anything else can teach you. You will learn how to pick data, how it impacts model quality, way of thinking, scores, personality. If training your own is too much, start with a completed pretrain and toy with it.

2. Building a harness around a completion model - I'd put this as second best to understand the inner worlds of LLM's. It helps you build intuition around how prompting really works, how they form the answers, how to build around that. Then you can do an SFT for your own harness.

3. Building a harness and an orchestrator around finished models - this takes the bronze. It teaches you how harnesses, agents and swarms actually work, how they shape the model's thoughts and actions, how models interact with them, how they can be applied and how they can work without humans.
